name: Ataja
title: Man from the tribe of Judah in Nehemiah's time
summary: Ataliah was a descendant of Perez through the tribe of Judah, who settled in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile. He is listed in the book of Nehemiah among the prominent men who took up residence in the holy city as part of an organized effort to repopulate Jerusalem. His lineage traces back through Uzzi, Zechariah, Amariah, Shephatiah, and Mahalalel to Perez, placing him within a significant and recognized branch of the tribe of Judah. Repopulating Jerusalem with prominent representatives from various families was essential for restoring the city as the religious and administrative center of the Jewish community in the post-exilic period.
roles: member of the tribe of Judah

keyEvents.title: Settlement in Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: Ataja was among the prominent men from the tribe of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after returning from exile. This was part of an organized effort to repopulate the city, where leaders settled in the city and others were chosen by lot.

keyEvents.title: Genealogy documented
keyEvents.description: Ataja's lineage is detailed in Nehemiah: he was the son of Uzzi, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, from the sons of Perez in the tribe of Judah. This careful documentation highlights his belonging to an important and recognized branch of Judah.

keyEvents.title: Possible parallel in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: In 1 Chronicles there is a similar list of those who lived in Jerusalem, with representatives from the sons of Perez in the tribe of Judah. The relationship between this list and Nehemiah 11 is debated among scholars, and it is unclear whether it refers to the same person or a parallel tradition.

versions.title: Levite in the time of Nehemiah
versions.reason: [major] The title calls Ataiah a 'Levite', but according to Nehemiah 11:4 he belonged to the tribe of Judah (from the sons of Perez), not the tribe of Levi. The title is therefore incorrect.; [major] The role 'leader' is somewhat imprecise. Ataiah is primarily described as a prominent resident/settler in Jerusalem from the tribe of Judah, not necessarily as a leader in a formal sense. A more appropriate role would be 'resident of Jerusalem' or 'tribal head'.; [major] According to Nehemiah 11:4, Ataiah's father was Uzzi, but the full lineage is Ataiah son of Uzzi, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel. The ID 'uzzi' may refer to several people, but it is correct based on the text.; [minor] The genealogy is mentioned in verse 4 alone in Nehemiah 11. Verse 5 concerns Maaseiah, another person. The reference should be limited to verse 4.; [minor] The description contains a grammatical error: 'after the Babylonian captivity' should be 'after the Babylonian exile'.; [minor] The reference to 1 Chron 9:4 mentions an Ataiah, but it is unclear whether this is the same person. This should be phrased more cautiously.; [minor] The summary states that Ataiah was 'a man from the tribe of Judah' but the title says 'Levite'. The summary is correct but should be harmonized with a corrected title.; [minor] There are no footnotes on, for example, the meaning of the name Ataiah, the historical context for the repopulation of Jerusalem, and the relationship between the lists in Nehemiah 11 and 1 Chronicles 9.

versions.reason: [minor] The description of the genealogy is somewhat confusing because the order can be misunderstood. According to Neh 11:4, Ataja is the son of Ussija, son of Sekareja, son of Amarja, son of Sjefatja, son of Mahalalel, from the sons of Peres. The current phrasing "through Sekareja, Amarja, Sjefatja and Mahalalel" may give the impression that these are collateral lines. A clearer formulation would be to say "son of Ussija, son of Sekareja, son of Amarja, son of Sjefatja, son of Mahalalel".; [minor] In 1 Chr 9:4 a "Utai, son of Ammihud" from the sons of Peres is mentioned – not necessarily a person named Ataja. The parallel between Neh 11:4 and 1 Chr 9:4 is debated, but the names do not match directly. It should be clarified more clearly that the parallel concerns the list/context rather than an identical name.

footnotes.text: The name Ataja (Hebrew: עֲתָיָה) means 'the Lord has helped' or 'Yahweh is helper'. It is a theophoric name expressing trust in God's care and help.

Nehemiah 11:1–2 describes how the leaders settled in Jerusalem, and one out of ten people from the rest of the nation was chosen by lot to live in the city. Those who volunteered were blessed by the people. This was necessary because Jerusalem had a sparse population after the exile.

The lists in Nehemiah 11 and 1 Chronicles 9 share many parallels, but their relationship is debated among scholars. Some believe they reflect different time periods, while others see them as variants of the same source.
Peres (Hebrew: פֶּרֶץ) was one of the sons of Judah and Tamar (Gen 38:29). The Peres clan was a prominent branch of the tribe of Judah, and King David also belonged to this lineage.

The repopulation of Jerusalem after the exile was a strategic and religious measure. A populated capital was essential for securing temple service, defending the city, and restoring Judah as a viable community under Persian rule.

Under Persian rule, Jerusalem served as the center of the province of Yehud. Archaeological findings show that during this period the city was significantly smaller than before its destruction in 586 BC, supporting the need for an active repopulation policy as described in Nehemiah 11.
